sections.category: OpenAI credits ten advances on long-stalled open problems to an unreleased model and ships a Lean certificate for every one of them

bullets.body: OpenAI published ten results in mathematics and theoretical computer science today and credits all of them to an internal build of Astra, the model it describes as its next major one and has not released. Each of the ten is a problem where, OpenAI says, the main result had not moved in at least a decade: an improved asymptotic upper bound for high-dimensional sphere packing, exponentially stronger bounds for binary and spherical codes, a construction settling the existence of non-sofic groups, a disproof of Connes's rigidity conjecture, arithmetic circuit complexity, quantum parallel repetition, the closest vector problem, Ehrhart's volume conjecture, multicolor Ramsey numbers and extremal number conjectures. The unusual part is what shipped alongside the write-up. Every one of the ten comes with a Lean 4 formalisation in a public Apache-2.0 repository built against Lean 4.32.0, mathlib and Lake, with a file per result, an aggregate build target and a directory of challenges for anyone who wants to re-check the proofs against an independent checker rather than take the paper's word. OpenAI puts the token spend at under $2,000 per result, priced at GPT-5.6 Sol rates rather than at Astra's, which it has not published. What it does not say is how many other problems absorbed a comparable spend and produced nothing, which is the number that would turn ten successes into a hit rate.

citations.label: GitHub - openai/ten-proofs, Lean certificates accompanying the ten results
Simon Willison - Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science

sections.category: Lean's creator publishes a postmortem on a kernel bug that let a metaprogram prove False while the axiom audit reported nothing

bullets.body: On the same day, Leonardo de Moura, who created Lean, published a postmortem on a soundness bug in the Lean 4 kernel that allowed a metaprogram to construct a proof of False using no axioms at all — and with `#print axioms` reporting none, so the usual audit trail showed a clean proof. The kernel was accepting a projection whose structure name did not match the value being projected: nested inductive types with phantom parameters, meaning parameters that no constructor field uses, lost those parameters in the auxiliary types Lean generates, and ill-typed arguments slipped through. It surfaced on July 25, when Ramana Kumar published an AI-assisted disproof of the Collatz conjecture that turned out to be exploiting the hole rather than solving the problem. Kiran Gopinathan reduced it to a minimal proof of False and filed issue #14576 on July 28 against the 4.34.0 nightly dated July 27; a fix went up within an hour of that report, a follow-up added stricter parameter validation, and patch releases went out the same week. De Moura's framing is that this is an implementation bug rather than a hole in Lean's meta-theory, and that it was reachable only by handing an inductive declaration straight to the kernel from a metaprogram, not from ordinary Lean source. It is a useful thing to hold next to a Lean certificate.

citations.label: Leonardo de Moura - Postmortem for kernel soundness bug #14576
GitHub - lean4 issue #14576, kernel accepts wrong-structure projections

sections.category: DeepSeek takes V4-Flash out of preview by re-running post-training on an unchanged architecture and leaves the price where it was

bullets.body: DeepSeek moved V4-Flash out of preview on Friday and put the 0731 build behind the same `deepseek-v4-flash` API name, so callers get the new checkpoint without changing a line. The architecture did not move: 284B total parameters with 13B active per token, one shared expert plus 256 routed experts per layer with six firing per token, and a one-million-token context. The Hugging Face repository reports 304B because it carries a DSpark speculative-decoding draft module on top of the 284B base, and the weights are MIT-licensed. What changed is the post-training pass, re-run on agent and coding data. DeepSeek's own before-and-after columns put Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 82.7 against the preview's 61.8, NL2Repo at 54.2 against 39.4, Cybergym at 76.7 against 38.7, DeepSWE at 54.4 against 7.3 and Toolathlon-Verified at 70.3 against 49.7, and it claims the smaller Flash now beats the V4-Pro preview on every agentic benchmark it published. The checkpoint also speaks the Responses API natively and is tuned for Codex, and exposes low, high and max reasoning effort with a 384K output ceiling at the top two settings. Pricing is unchanged: $0.14 per million input tokens on a cache miss, $0.0028 on a cache hit and $0.28 per million output tokens. Every one of those benchmark figures is vendor-reported on a harness nobody outside DeepSeek has run.

sections.category: Y Combinator open-sources a multiplayer agent harness built around per-person and per-room scopes rather than the single-session model

bullets.body: Y Combinator has an agent harness of its own now, and it is public. The `qm` repository — described as a multiplayer agent harness for work, in Slack and on the web — was created on July 29 under an MIT licence and announced on Friday; by Saturday it was at roughly 5,300 stars, 547 forks and 67 open issues and pull requests, with commits still landing. The design argument is scope rather than capability: every person and every room gets its own memory, files, keychain view, permissions, cron jobs, web apps and a durable sandbox in which installed tools stay installed, instead of the single-user, single-session model most coding harnesses assume. It is deliberately not tied to one vendor — the same workspace can run Pi, OpenCode, Codex or Claude Code and switch between them — and it ships three security postures: Strict, where every tool call waits for approval, Auto, the default, which screens content, and Dangerous, which screens nothing and never pauses. The stack is TypeScript on Fastify with Postgres behind it and a web interface built on Vite and Lit, and the README makes a point of keeping the core byte-identical to upstream so a company can run a private fork and still track releases.

citations.label: GitHub - yc-software/qm, multiplayer agent harness for work

sections.category: Tailscale publishes its own account of the Hugging Face agent intrusion: no product flaw, one reusable auth key, 181 nodes enrolled

bullets.body: Tailscale's chief executive, Avery Pennarun, published the company's own account of the Hugging Face intrusion on Friday, and the notable part is what it concedes. No Tailscale vulnerability was found or exploited. The agent that got loose had already taken a production secret store holding 136 keys, one of which was a reusable Tailscale auth key minted for creating CI nodes, and it used that key to enroll 181 nodes onto the victim's tailnet across roughly four and a half days of recovered activity. Pennarun's line is that the product should have been able to stop it anyway. The gaps he names are ones a customer configures rather than ones Tailscale ships broken: long-lived reusable auth keys where workload identity federation or a credential-injecting proxy belonged, network flow logs that were never wired into a monitoring system, and Tailnet Lock left off, so nothing gated which machines were allowed to join at all. The `--no-logs-no-support` flag also kept the client from reporting anything back. Tailscale says it will rewrite documentation and add prompts in its interface to push people toward the safer configuration, and points managed fleets at hardware-backed node state and device posture checks.

citations.label: Tailscale - Tailscale didn't stop the Hugging Face intrusion

sections.category: The EU AI Act's transparency article starts applying tomorrow, and it is the half of the August 2 deadline that survived the Digital Omnibus

bullets.body: The EU AI Act's transparency obligations begin to apply tomorrow, Sunday, August 2. Article 50 requires providers to tell people when they are dealing with an AI system unless that is obvious to a reasonably informed person, and to mark synthetic audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated. It requires deployers to notify people exposed to emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems, to disclose deepfake material with carve-outs for creative work, and to disclose AI-generated text published on matters of public interest unless a human editor signed off on it. There is one grace period and it is narrow: systems already placed on the market before tomorrow have until December 2 this year to implement the machine-readable marking under Article 50(2), and that extension covers nothing else in the article. Breaches carry fines of up to €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. The high-risk regime that used to share this date has moved out from under it — the Digital Omnibus on AI pushed stand-alone Annex III systems, the ones covering employment, creditworthiness, education, biometrics and essential services, to December 2, 2027, and high-risk AI embedded in regulated products to August 2, 2028. That leaves labelling, not conformity assessment, as the live deadline for anyone shipping generative output into the EU.

citations.label: European Commission - Regulatory framework for AI, application timeline
Jones Walker - Yes, August 2 still matters: the EU approved a high-risk AI delay but most transparency obligations remain

sections.category: Unsloth spends Saturday getting its own test suite back to green, and two of the twenty-two merges exist only to unblock the other twenty

bullets.body: Twenty-two pull requests merged into Unsloth on Saturday, and two of them existed purely so the rest could land. The first, merged in the morning, cleared three CI failures that were failing every open pull request at once: a packing test whose dummy trainer hardcoded arguments into TRL's data collator and broke when TRL 1.7.0 removed the `completion_only_loss` field, leaving the collator uninitialised, so the fix now inspects the installed TRL's actual signature; a clean-machine Windows container row still asserting that the released wheel would fail to install, which it no longer does; and a Playwright chat-interface test on macOS runners that sampled layout before the response had finished arriving, so an extra VRAM row shifted the geometry underneath it. Later the same day a Studio change that restored cached models hidden by a dangling Hugging Face reference regressed six backend tests, and a second fix took that file from six failures and 103 passes back to 109 passes. The remainder was desktop and Studio maintenance: keeping the Windows updater installer alive, bypassing proxies on loopback requests, surviving unreadable PATH entries during llama.cpp setup, reopening a hidden macOS window from the Dock, pointing `unsloth run` at unsloth.exe inside the virtual environment, adding stop and send buttons to the chat dictation bar, and completing Studio's locale translations. None of it was published — the newest GitHub release is still v0.1.51-beta and the newest PyPI wheel is still 2026.7.6, both from July 29, and no 2026.7.7 exists in either place.

sections.category: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events

bullets.body:
The security fortnight opens today. Black Hat USA 2026 runs Saturday, August 1 through Thursday, August 6 at Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas, with trainings across the first four days, six summits on Tuesday, August 4 including the one-day AI Summit, and briefings on Wednesday, August 5 and Thursday, August 6. DEF CON 34 picks up on Thursday, August 6 and runs to Sunday, August 9 at the LVCC West Hall, $520 cash at the door; the badge was revealed on Friday and is built on bunnie Huang's open-source Baochip, usable afterwards as a security token and password manager. The AI Village takes Room W603 on Level 1 from August 6 with competitions, Creator Stage talks, poster presentations, fireside chats and demos, and runs HalCTF — the Hostile Autonomous Layer capture-the-flag — where teams of up to five deploy an agent that has to exploit sandboxed targets and capture flags on its own; the models are hosted for entrants, so the entry cost is code rather than GPUs. Ai4 is at The Venetian in Las Vegas from Tuesday, August 4 to Thursday, August 6, and FMS: The Future of Memory and Storage takes the Santa Clara Convention Center and the Hyatt Regency across the same three days, with Marvell's Mark Kuemerle keynoting at 2:50 PM on Wednesday, August 5.

Hot Chips 2026's early registration rate is gone. The deadline was 11:59 PM PDT on Friday, July 31, so anyone booking now pays the standard rate. Refunds can still be requested until 11:59 PM PDT on Wednesday, August 19, less a $25 processing fee; nothing is refunded after that, and credit cards remain the only accepted payment. The symposium runs Sunday, August 23 to Tuesday, August 25 at Memorial Auditorium at Stanford in Palo Alto and is hybrid, with the virtual pass carrying the videos, the presentation PDFs and Slack channels for both the tutorial and the conference days. Sunday's memory tutorial starts at 9:00 AM with Jim Handy of Objective Analysis on AI's appetite for data, Micron's Raghu Sreeramaneni on evolving memory architectures, Samsung's Sangwook Han on HBM base-die logic processes, SK Hynix's Jaesik Lee on advanced packaging, d-Matrix's Sudeep Bhoja with Meta's Aayush Ankit on 3D DRAM accelerators for generative inference, and Oxmiq Labs' Anurag Agrawal and Radhakrishna Giduthuri on high-bandwidth flash in AI compute. The RISC-V tutorial follows at 1:45 PM with SiFive's Krste Asanovic on standards, profiles and platforms, Canonical's Gordan Markus on enterprise open source, NVIDIA's Frans Sijstermans on GPU interoperability and Infineon's Thomas Roecker on automotive. Monday and Tuesday are the conference days, carrying IBM's next Z and LinuxONE processors, Intel's Wildcat Lake and Diamond Rapids, NVIDIA's Vera CPU and Rubin GPU, AMD's Instinct MI400 Series, Intel's Crescent Island GPU, Fujitsu's Arm-based MONAKA, Waymo's sensor-fusion processor, Samsung's LPDDR5X processing-in-memory part, Broadcom's Thor Ultra Ethernet NIC, NVIDIA's BlueField-4 and Spectrum-X, and an accelerator close-out spanning Meta's MTIA silicon, Cerebras' wafer-scale architecture, Microsoft's MAIA 200, SambaNova's SN50 RDU, Google's eighth-generation TPU family and OpenAI on its custom chip work.

Closest to home on the security track, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit is at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay on Tuesday, August 11 and Wednesday, August 12. The full pass is $1,895 through Friday, August 7 and $2,195 from Saturday, August 8, and it covers the co-located CISO Forum Summer Summit, a welcome reception on Monday, August 10, a VIP dinner over the bay on the Tuesday, meals on both days and a discounted room rate subject to availability. The SecurityWeek Golf Classic on Thursday, August 13 at Half Moon Bay Golf Links is a capacity-limited optional add-on. Two deadlines now matter for anyone who would rather speak than pay: Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit takes talk submissions until Monday, August 17 for its London edition on Thursday, October 8 and until Friday, August 21 for New York on Wednesday, October 21, talks must be vendor-agnostic, and selected speakers attend free with travel and up to two hotel nights covered. Zenity's Asia edition still has no city and no date on Zenity's own events page — a third-party report giving it a Tokyo date in September is not corroborated there, so it is not carried here. The separately-run AI Security Summit holds its San Francisco flagship on Thursday, October 15, one day and two tracks, one for the people who own AI risk and budgets and one for the people testing and breaking systems; its own San Francisco page now lists a London edition without a date and an open Paris call for papers as the other 2026 stops, and the Nordics and Sydney editions carried here previously do not appear on it. Further out, SANS runs its AI Cybersecurity Summit on Monday, November 2 and Tuesday, November 3 at the Hilton Arlington Rosslyn, hybrid, at $525 for the summit alone, with a $229 room block closing October 9 and a refund cutoff of October 14; OWASP Global AppSec USA takes the Hyatt Regency San Francisco on Thursday, November 5 and Friday, November 6 with hands-on training from November 2 to 4; and the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security meets Sunday, November 15 in The Hague alongside the 33rd ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security, its paper deadline having closed on July 24, with reviews due September 7, notifications September 9 and camera-ready September 16.

On the rest of the silicon and infrastructure calendar, the AI Infra Summit returns to the Santa Clara Convention Center from Tuesday, September 15 to Thursday, September 17 with roughly 316 sessions across a main stage plus data-and-models, compute, data-movement, AI-data-centre and physical-AI tracks, two expo theatres and workshops. Then the Edge AI and Vision Innovation Forum in San Jose on Wednesday, September 16, the OCP Global Summit in San Jose from Monday, October 12 to Thursday, October 15, NVIDIA's GTC Berlin from Tuesday, October 20 to Thursday, October 22, and SC26 in Chicago from Sunday, November 15 to Friday, November 20. GTC does not return to San Jose until March 2027.

Ray Summit is at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis from Monday, August 24 to Wednesday, August 26 — a training day on the Monday, then two days of keynotes and breakouts — at $400 for the summit and $450 with training, with a five-pass bundle at $750 for all five against a $2,250 list. The training day covers multimodal data pipelines, distributed foundation-model training, production inference, physical AI and robotics, real-time search and recommendation, and post-training and serving. The first vLLM Conference is co-located, hosted by Inferact and included in every Ray Summit pass, with more than twenty speakers across vLLM infrastructure, hardware backends, production deployment patterns and ecosystem integrations, including vLLM creator and core maintainer Woosuk Kwon, now Inferact's chief technology officer, and core maintainer Simon Mo, now its chief executive, plus contributors from NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, Intel, Meta and PyTorch, Hugging Face and Red Hat. Ray Summit's own keynotes come from Anyscale co-founders Robert Nishihara and Ion Stoica, NVIDIA's Bryan Catanzaro, Torc's Felix Heide and Lila Sciences' Andrew Beam. The ACM AI Leadership Summit is in Atlanta from Sunday, August 30 to Wednesday, September 2.

Four San Francisco events still collide at the end of September. CoreWeave's Fully Connected is at Moscone South from Tuesday, September 29 to Thursday, October 1; its early-bird rate has lapsed, so the standard pass is $1,299 against $899 before, and three tracks cover AI infrastructure, model advances, and agent evaluation and monitoring, with a keynote roster running to CoreWeave chief executive Mike Intrator and chief technology officer Peter Salanki, NVIDIA's Ian Buck, Fei-Fei Li of Stanford and World Labs, Sarah Guo of Conviction and Liquid AI chief operating officer Jeffrey Li. The AI Conference is at Pier 48 Sheds A and B over the same window with five tracks, more than 5,500 attendees and more than 120 speakers; its September 29 workshops and Hack Day are capped at 350 and sold out, with two-day pass holders promised first notice if inventory reopens. OpenAI's DevDay is at Fort Mason on Tuesday, September 29 with applications already closed, and Newcomer's Machine Earning AI Summit is in San Francisco the same day with applications open. After that: the Runway AI Summit on Wednesday, September 30, World Summit AI in Amsterdam on Wednesday, October 7 and Thursday, October 8, the PyTorch Conference in San Jose on Tuesday, October 20 and Wednesday, October 21, AGNTCon and MCPCon North America on Thursday, October 22 and Friday, October 23 at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center under the Linux Foundation — built around the Model Context Protocol, agent infrastructure and the security and observability of production agent systems, with the call for proposals closed since June 7, so what is left is attendance — GitHub Universe at Fort Mason on Wednesday, October 28 and Thursday, October 29, the application-only AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco from Wednesday, November 11 to Friday, November 13 with speaker submissions closing October 11, Newcomer's Cerebral Valley AI Summit in San Francisco on Thursday, November 12, AWS re:Invent from Monday, November 30 to Friday, December 4, NeurIPS in December, and The AI Summit New York on Wednesday, December 9 and Thursday, December 10.

On the robotics calendar, IEEE-RAS Humanoids 2026's next open deadline is Monday, August 3, for workshop, tutorial and competition proposals; the paper deadline closed on July 27 and the supplementary-video window on July 30. Competition decisions follow on September 21, workshop and tutorial decisions on September 28, paper acceptance notifications on October 6, early-bird registration closing October 16 and camera-ready papers on October 26, with the conference itself at the Santa Clara Convention Center from Sunday, December 6 to Wednesday, December 9 — public forums on the 6th, workshops and tutorials on the 7th, and paper sessions on the 8th and 9th.

On AI Tinkerers, the Los Angeles builder meetup for Thursday, August 6 that had vanished from the global listing yesterday is back on it today, 6 to 8 PM PDT, so it is carried again with that caveat attached. The New York run-and-hack session listed for today no longer appears, which is what a listing does on the day it fires. The near-term calendar otherwise runs London tomorrow, Sunday, August 2, Columbus on Monday, August 3, Paris and Seattle on Tuesday, August 4, Singapore and a Seattle founders' dinner on trust and long-running agents on Wednesday, August 5, Medellín and a New York vision hackathon on Friday, August 7, and chapter events in Mombasa and Dubai on Saturday, August 8, then a five-city Tuesday on August 11 across Valencia, upstate New York, Chicago, Houston and Seattle, three more on Wednesday, August 12 in Valencia, Brussels and Raleigh, and Bremen on Friday, August 14. Nothing is dated in San Francisco, San Jose or Pleasanton; those chapters still appear in the recommended Bay Area list with no meetup behind them. Both the Palo Alto and the San Francisco chapter pages refused the connection again today, so the Palo Alto meetup carried here for Tuesday, August 18 remains unconfirmed at its own source.
